title: Richmond Regional Housing Framework
text:
About this update
This is the 2026 Data Update to the Richmond Regional Housing Framework, produced by HDAdvisors for the Partnership for Housing Affordability (PHA). It refreshes the 2022 Framework with the latest available data and reorganizes the findings around the region’s most pressing housing themes.






Note



This is a preliminary working draft for PHA review. Figures and findings are subject to revision as the analysis develops, and the site is not yet indexed for search. Reviewers can comment inline using Hypothesis.


The update covers the PlanRVA region — Charles City, Chesterfield, Goochland, Hanover, Henrico, New Kent, and Powhatan counties; the City of Richmond; and the Town of Ashland. Regional analysis centers on the four primary jurisdictions (Chesterfield, Hanover, Henrico, and Richmond); the five secondary localities receive individual local summaries.
Five preliminary-findings sections anchor the update:

Housing demand
Homeownership market
Rental market
Housing gap
Cost burden and instability

Each section leads with what changed since the 2022 Framework and organizes its findings by takeaway rather than by data source.

title: 1  Housing demand
text:
1.1 The region has added nearly 70,000 residents since the 2020 census
Figure 1.1: The region has added nearly 70,000 residents since the 2020 census

title: 1  Housing demand
text:
The region added nearly 70,000 residents between the 2020 census and the 2025 population estimate, growth of 6.2 percent in five years.
Every year from 2020 to 2025 added population, with the largest single-year gains in 2024 (+17,600) and 2025 (+14,000).
Longer term, the 8-locality region has grown steadily since 2000, from 865,941 residents to 1,120,304 at the 2020 census (+29%) — context for the recent estimates above.

title: 1  Housing demand
section: 1.2 Migration, not natural increase, now powers the region’s growth
text:
1.2 Migration, not natural increase, now powers the region’s growth








Figure 1.2: Migration, not births, is driving the region’s population growth






Net migration has delivered the large majority of the region’s growth every year since 2021, peaking at roughly 15,500 net movers in 2024.
Natural change (births minus deaths) has stayed small — under about 2,100 residents per year regionwide — reflecting an aging population and post-pandemic mortality patterns.
The region’s demand pressure is therefore driven by households arriving from elsewhere, who need housing immediately upon arrival.
The 2020 estimate period covers only April-June 2020 and is omitted from the chart.

title: 1  Housing demand
section: 1.3 Every primary locality is projected to keep growing through 2050
text:
1.3 Every primary locality is projected to keep growing through 2050








Figure 1.3: Chesterfield is projected to pass 500,000 residents by 2050






Chesterfield is projected to grow 43% by 2050, reaching about 520,000 residents — up from the 38% growth projected in the 2022 Framework.
Henrico (+25%, to 416,000), Hanover (+27%, to 139,000), and Richmond city (+22%, to 276,000) all continue growing, with no primary locality projected to plateau.
The full 8-locality region is projected to reach about 1,472,000 residents by 2050, growth of 31% over the 2020 census.
Among secondary localities, New Kent has the fastest projected growth rate (+72%), while Charles City is the only locality projected to lose population (-19%).

title: 1  Housing demand
section: 1.4 The region is aging, and more seniors are living alone
text:
1.4 The region is aging, and more seniors are living alone








Figure 1.4: Nearly one in three residents is now 55 or older






Residents 55 and older make up 30% of the region’s population, and residents 65 and older make up 17%.
The 25-34 age group is the region’s single largest — prime household-formation years, which converts directly into near-term housing demand.
53,585 households — 12% of all households regionwide — are seniors 65+ living alone, a group with distinct needs for smaller, accessible, and lower-maintenance homes.
Women outnumber men in the 75+ group, so older single-person households are disproportionately older women.

title: 1  Housing demand
section: 1.5 Median household income has kept climbing since 2019, in every locality
text:
1.5 Median household income has kept climbing since 2019, in every locality








Figure 1.5: Median household income has kept climbing since 2019, in every locality






Every locality’s median household income rose at least 23 percent since 2019, and New Kent’s rose 40 percent.
Richmond city’s median rose 37 percent since 2019 — from $47,250 to $64,587 — yet it remains the lowest in the region, at roughly half of New Kent’s $123,314.
The fastest growth since 2019 was in New Kent (+40%); the slowest was in Chesterfield (+23%).
Going back to 2014, every locality’s median has risen at least 40% in nominal terms — a full decade of income growth that predates this recent acceleration.
Each vintage is expressed in its own survey-year dollars, so these changes are nominal; part of the increase reflects inflation.







NoteData caveats



Population estimates for 2020-2025 are Census Bureau Vintage 2025 figures and will be revised in future vintages. Weldon Cooper projections are the 2025 release, benchmarked to the 2020 census. ACS income medians are 5-year averages in each vintage’s own survey-year dollars — comparisons across vintages are nominal, not inflation-adjusted. The 2022 Framework baseline used 2016-2020 ACS and the prior Weldon Cooper release, so “Since 2022” comparisons reflect both real change and vintage revisions.

title: 2  Homeownership market
text:
2.1 Homeownership rates rose almost everywhere since 2019
Figure 2.1: Homeownership rates rose almost everywhere since 2019

title: 2  Homeownership market
text:
The region as a whole is 67.0% owner-occupied in 2024, just above the statewide rate of 67.3 percent.
The three smallest counties posted the largest gains since 2019: New Kent (+6.2 points, to 92.6 percent), Powhatan (+3.1, to 93.2 percent), and Charles City (+2.4, to 86.3 percent).
Hanover is the only locality where the owner share fell since 2019, dipping slightly from 82.5 to 82.1 percent.
The four core localities barely moved since 2019 — Richmond city (43.5 percent) remains the region’s only majority-renter jurisdiction, and Hanover (82.1 percent) the highest among them.
All plotted owner-household estimates are High reliability (CV at or below 15); the dataset’s only Medium cells are 2024 renter counts in New Kent and Powhatan, and do not appear in this figure.

title: 2  Homeownership market
section: 2.2 Home prices are up 65 percent since the start of 2020
text:
2.2 Home prices are up 65 percent since the start of 2020








Figure 2.2: Home prices are up 65 percent since the start of 2020






The median sale price reached $435,000 in July 2026, up 65% from $264,000 in January 2020 (nominal dollars).
Prices kept climbing after 2022: the 12-month average is up 27% since January 2022, from about $327,997 to $416,357.
The steepest appreciation came in 2020-2022, when the 12-month average rose from roughly $268,541 to $327,997 — growth has continued since, but at roughly half that pace.
Monthly medians are seasonal and noisy; the 12-month average, shown here since 2020, is the better read on trend.

title: 2  Homeownership market
section: 2.3 Home values are up at least a third in every locality since 2019
text:
2.3 Home values are up at least a third in every locality since 2019








Figure 2.3: Home values are up at least a third in every locality since 2019






2024 median home values span more than a two-to-one range across the region, from $241,400 in Charles City to $500,600 in Goochland.
Richmond city posted the fastest growth since 2019 — up 53 percent, from $230,500 to $353,000 — continuing to erode its historical role as the region’s lower-cost ownership market.
Every locality gained at least 33 percent since 2019, and the four core localities all now exceed the $350,000 mark.
Four of the eight localities sit above the statewide median of $383,700: Goochland, Powhatan, Hanover, and New Kent.
Medians are locality-level ACS estimates and do not sum or average to a regional figure; all plotted values are High reliability.

title: 2  Homeownership market
section: 2.4 Multifamily permits have outpaced single-family in three of the last four years
text:
2.4 Multifamily permits have outpaced single-family in three of the last four years








Figure 2.4: Multifamily permits have outpaced single-family in three of the last four years






Since 2020, multifamily permits are up 69%, from 2,770 to 4,677 units, while single-family permits fell 21%, from 4,825 to 3,792.
2022 was the first year in the 2000-2025 record that regional multifamily volume exceeded single-family (5,804 vs 3,946 units) — a pattern that repeated in 2023 and again in 2025.
Total regional permitting peaked in 2022 at 9,750 units, more than double the post-recession low of 2,186 in 2009, and has eased only modestly since.
The 2022 Framework’s Fig 5.4 baseline for Chesterfield single-family permits — 545 in 2010, 2,202 in 2020 — matches this pull exactly; same metric, same years, no vintage shift.

title: 2  Homeownership market
section: 2.5 Mortgage rates have more than doubled since their 2020-2021 low
text:
2.5 Mortgage rates have more than doubled since their 2020-2021 low








Figure 2.5: Mortgage rates have more than doubled since their 2020-2021 low






The 30-year fixed rate fell to a low of 2.68% in December 2020, peaked at 7.62% in October 2023, and stands at 6.54% as of July 2026 — more than double the 2020-2021 low.
Home prices did not pause for the rate run-up: the median sale price rose from $264,000 in January 2020 to $435,000 by July 2026, the 65 percent gain covered above.
Higher rates and higher prices are compounding rather than offsetting — a fixed monthly housing budget buys much less home today than it did when rates sat near 3 percent.
The mortgage rate is Freddie Mac’s national PMMS survey, not Richmond-specific; both series here are nominal, unadjusted for inflation.







NoteTo be added



Sales inventory and months of supply. Active listings, new listings, and months-of-supply trends from the regional MLS.

title: 3  Rental market
text:
3.1 Median rent has climbed fastest since 2019, in every locality
Figure 3.1: Median rent has climbed fastest since 2019, in every locality

title: 3  Rental market
text:
Every locality posted a higher median gross rent in 2024 than in 2019, and in all eight the 2019-to-2024 increase outpaced the full 2014-to-2019 span.
New Kent had the region’s highest 2024 median rent at $1,721, up 70 percent since 2019 alone — the sharpest increase in the region.
Richmond city’s median rent rose 34 percent since 2019, from $1,025 to $1,372 — yet stayed below the statewide median of $1,579.
Powhatan had the slowest rent growth since 2019, at 19 percent; small-county medians (New Kent, Powhatan, Goochland, Charles City) carry wide margins of error and describe small renter stocks.
All figures are nominal dollars; inflation-adjusted comparisons come with the cost-burden analysis.

title: 3  Rental market
section: 3.2 Renter shares held steady since 2019, except in the smallest counties
text:
3.2 Renter shares held steady since 2019, except in the smallest counties








Figure 3.2: Renter shares held steady since 2019, except in the smallest counties






The region added roughly 10,656 renter households between 2019 and 2024, a 8% increase — faster growth than the full prior five years.
Richmond city drove the gain, adding about 7,107 renter households since 2019 — roughly NA of the regional increase — though its renter share held near 56% because total households grew just as fast.
Chesterfield and Hanover renter counts grew steadily since 2019, but both counties remain more than three-quarters owner-occupied.
The three smallest counties — Charles City, New Kent, and Powhatan — each lost renter households since 2019, deepening the ownership tilt of the outer region; New Kent’s renter count fell 37 percent.
Over the full decade, the region added 20,309 renter households (15%) — most of that growth came in the last five years.

title: 3  Rental market
section: 3.3 Asking rents are up 28 percent since 2020, even as the market has loosened
text:
3.3 Asking rents are up 28 percent since 2020, even as the market has loosened








Figure 3.3: Asking rents are up 28 percent since 2020, even as the market has loosened






Regional average asking rent reached $1,583 in 2026 Q2, up 28% from $1,235 in early 2020.
The market was tightest in early 2022 — vacancy near 6%, the low point of the period — and rents have risen another 11% since then, to $1,583.
Vacancy has since climbed to 8.5% in 2026 Q2, above where it stood at the start of 2020, as new deliveries caught up with and then outpaced demand.
CoStar coverage is professionally managed multifamily; New Kent and Charles City have only a handful of tracked properties, so locality-level trends there are not meaningful.







NoteSince 2022



The 2022 Framework flagged a regional average asking rent of $1,395 in early 2022 as a two-decade high with vacancy near 5%. Rents have since risen another 11% to $1,583, but the market has loosened: vacancy is now 8.5%, and rent growth has slowed sharply. The 2022 Framework also reported a net loss of renter households from 2016 to 2020 (with a COVID-era data caveat); the 2020–2024 ACS instead shows renter households growing across the region.

title: 3  Rental market
section: 3.4 Nearly 30 percent of the region’s assisted units expire within a decade
text:
3.4 Nearly 30 percent of the region’s assisted units expire within a decade








Figure 3.4: Nearly 30 percent of the region’s assisted units expire within a decade






About 6,491 of the region’s 22,781 active assisted units — 28% — carry subsidies expiring by 2035, the window preservation funders typically prioritize.
Three-quarters of tracked properties (152 of 201) are LIHTC-financed, holding 17,465 units; LIHTC’s own affordability period can lapse independently of the subsidy end date tracked here, a second layer of risk this figure does not fully capture.
Richmond city and Henrico account for the large majority of tracked properties (117 and 47 of 201); Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan have no NHPD-tracked assisted multifamily properties at all.
About 3,336 units carry no listed subsidy end date, mostly public housing and HOME-assisted properties whose affordability commitments do not lapse the same way project-based subsidies do.

title: 3  Rental market
section: 3.5 Housing Choice Vouchers grew as public housing kept shrinking
text:
3.5 Housing Choice Vouchers grew as public housing kept shrinking








Figure 3.5: Housing Choice Vouchers grew as public housing kept shrinking






Housing Choice Vouchers grew 15% since 2020, from 5,910 to 6,822 units, while public housing fell 13%, from 3,706 to 3,226 — a policy-relevant shift from project-based to tenant-based assistance.
Regional voucher utilization slipped from 91 percent occupied in 2020 to 87 percent in 2024, even as the voucher supply grew — more vouchers issued, a slightly larger share sitting unused at any given time.
Project-based Section 8 (5,763 units in 2024) and the small 202/PRAC and 811/PRAC senior- and disability-designated programs (222 and 69 units) have stayed essentially flat since 2020.
Richmond city and Henrico hold the large majority of the region’s assisted units; Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan combined account for fewer than 40 units across all programs.







NoteTo be added



Submarket rents and vacancy. Submarket-level asking rent, vacancy, and new-construction rent detail, extending the regional trend above.

title: 5  Cost burden and instability
text:
5.1 Renter cost burden is climbing again since 2019
Figure 5.1: Renter cost burden is climbing again since 2019

title: 5  Cost burden and instability
text:
Renter cost burden eased to 50% by 2015–19 but has since climbed back to 51% in 2020–24 — a 1% increase in just five years.
Severe burden drives the recent rise: severely cost-burdened renters grew from 24.5 percent of all renters in 2015–19 to 26% in 2020–24.
Owners kept moving the opposite direction: the burdened owner share fell from 21% in 2015–19 to 20% in 2020–24, continuing a decade-long decline from 26 percent in 2010–14.
Because the renter population grew while the burdened share rose, the count of cost-burdened renter households climbed from 66,647 in 2015–19 to 73,767 in 2020–24 — a faster five-year rise than the change across the full prior decade.







ImportantSince 2022



The 2022 Framework reported cost-burdened renters up by almost 1,900 households and cost-burdened owners down by more than 7,200 since 2015 (Fig 10.1). This update finds the same split, larger on the renter side: burdened renter households up 10,349 (+16.3%) and burdened owner households down 7,742 (-11.4%) from 2010–2014 to 2020–2024. Caveat: the 2022 figures rode on the 2016–2020 ACS with a 2015 base year; this update compares non-overlapping 2010–2014 and 2020–2024 windows, so the magnitudes are directionally comparable but not measured on the same yardstick.

title: 5  Cost burden and instability
section: 5.2 Renter cost burden tops 50 percent in Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield alike
text:
5.2 Renter cost burden tops 50 percent in Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield alike








Figure 5.2: Renter cost burden tops 50 percent in Richmond, Henrico, and Chesterfield alike






Total renter cost burden is nearly uniform across the three largest localities: 52 percent in Chesterfield, 52 percent in Richmond, and 52 percent in Henrico — this is a regional condition, not a city problem.
Richmond has the largest severe tilt: 28 percent of city renters pay half or more of their income toward housing, against 24 percent in Henrico and 25 percent in Chesterfield.
Hanover is the outlier at 45 percent total renter burden, still well above the owner rate anywhere in the region.
The three largest localities all exceed the statewide renter burden rate of 49 percent; Hanover sits below it.
Estimates for Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan are suppressed: every renter burden cell in those localities carries a CV above 30 (Low reliability). Their small renter counts (roughly 300–1,300 renter households each) cannot support reliable shares at this cut; HUD’s CHAS tables cover them at coarser income-band cuts, in the AMI-band figure below.

title: 5  Cost burden and instability
section: 5.3 Cost burden is nearly universal below 30 percent of area median income
text:
5.3 Cost burden is nearly universal below 30 percent of area median income








Figure 5.3: Cost burden is nearly universal below 30 percent of area median income






NA of renters and NA of owners below 30 percent of area median income are cost-burdened, and most of them severely: NA of renters and NA of owners in this band pay half or more of income toward housing.
Burden falls sharply as income rises: by 50-80% AMI, NA of renters and NA of owners are burdened; above 100% AMI, fewer than NA of renters and NA of owners are.
Renters are more burdened than owners at every income band below 100% AMI, widest at the bottom of the scale.
These are regional totals pooled across all 8 Richmond region localities, so every income band here is measured at a reliable scale — including for Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan, whose renter counts are too small for the locality-level ACS cut above.

title: 5  Cost burden and instability
section: 5.4 Severe burden is rising in the counties, easing in Richmond
text:
5.4 Severe burden is rising in the counties, easing in Richmond








Figure 5.4: Severe burden is rising in the counties, easing in Richmond






Severe renter burden jumped in every primary locality except Richmond between 2015–19 and 2020–24: Chesterfield rose 4.2 points to 25 percent, Hanover rose 2.7 points to 22 percent, and Henrico rose 1.9 points to 24 percent.
Richmond moved the other way, easing from 30 percent in 2015–19 to 28 percent in 2020–24 — even as it still carries the region’s largest severe-burden caseload, about 15,800 renter households.
All four localities had dipped in 2015–19 before this recent runup, so the full-decade change looks smaller than the last five years alone.
Chesterfield added the most severely burdened renter households of any locality since 2015–19 — up about 1,600 (from 5,962 to 7,599), a 27 percent increase in five years.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
section: A.2 Geography definitions
text:
A.2 Geography definitions
The study area is the PlanRVA region, held constant across every source through vectors defined once in the project’s shared setup file.

Region (8 localities): Charles City, Chesterfield, Goochland, Hanover, Henrico, New Kent, and Powhatan counties, plus Richmond city. This is the full regional analysis universe.
Primary localities (4): Chesterfield, Hanover, Henrico, and Richmond city carry the core regional narrative.
Secondary localities (4): Charles City, Goochland, New Kent, and Powhatan appear in local summaries only, always with reliability flags (see below).
Town of Ashland: a Census place (not a county) inside Hanover County, so it is pulled at the place level (summary level 160) in ACS and CHAS scripts and treated as a ninth local-summary geography.
Virginia serves as the statewide benchmark.


PUMS geography
Microdata estimates use 2020-vintage PUMAs, which do not follow county lines everywhere.

Core-3 (the regional PUMS default): Chesterfield (3 PUMAs), Henrico (2), and Richmond city (2) — the three localities that tile cleanly into whole PUMAs.
Hanover cannot be isolated in PUMS. It is split across two multi-county PUMAs — one covering eastern Hanover with King William, New Kent, and Charles City; the other covering western Hanover with Goochland and Powhatan — so no PUMA combination yields Hanover alone. Hanover enters the analysis only through county-level ACS tables.
A full-region PUMA set (core-3 plus the two mixed outer PUMAs) exists for region-wide totals where the extra counties are acceptable; it is used sparingly and labeled when it appears.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
section: A.3 Estimate reliability
text:
A.3 Estimate reliability
ACS estimates for small geographies carry sampling error, flagged consistently from each estimate’s coefficient of variation (CV, on a 0–100 scale).

High reliability: CV at or below 15 — reported without qualification.
Medium reliability: CV above 15 and at or below 30 — reported with a footnote identifying the cell as medium-reliability.
Low reliability: CV above 30 — the cell is suppressed rather than reported.
Reliability treatment applies to every secondary-locality and Ashland ACS estimate in the report.
Small PIT and eviction counts are reported as counts with a volatility caveat, never converted to rates.

title: Appendix A — Data notes
section: A.4 Comparing to the 2022 Framework
text:
A.4 Comparing to the 2022 Framework
Every section compares its findings to the 2022 Richmond Regional Housing Framework, but the two cycles rest on different survey windows.

This update’s anchor is the 2020–2024 ACS 5-year; the 2022 Framework used the 2016–2020 ACS 5-year. Overlapping multi-year windows differ by construction, so some movement between the two reports is structural rather than real-world change.
Changes since 2022 are therefore logged and narrated, never gated: a large swing prompts human review but never fails a build.
The 2022 baseline figures are transcribed from the published 2022 report, not recomputed, so the comparison is always against the numbers PHA actually published.
The 2022 report defined “the region” as the four primary localities only; regional comparisons against the 2022 baseline carry that narrower scope rather than the full 8-locality region.
